verses.restored: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a Levite sojourning in remote parts of hill country of Ephraim. He took for himself a woman, a concubine, from Bethlehem in Judah.

familiar.text: And it came to pass in those days, when there was no king in Israel, that there was a certain Levite sojourning on the side of mount Ephraim, who took to him a concubine out of Bethlehemjudah.

modern.text: Now in those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.

familiar.text: And his concubine played the whore against him, and went away from him unto her father’s house to Bethlehemjudah, and was there four whole months.

modern.text: But she was unfaithful to him and left him to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. After she had been there four months,

familiar.text: And her husband arose, and went after her, to speak friendly unto her, and to bring her again, having his servant with him, and a couple of asses: and she brought him into her father’s house: and when the father of the damsel saw him, he rejoiced to meet him.

modern.text: her husband got up and went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back, taking his servant and a pair of donkeys. So the girl brought him into her father’s house, and when her father saw him, he gladly welcomed him.

familiar.text: And his father in law, the damsel’s father, retained him; and he abode with him three days: so they did eat and drink, and lodged there.

modern.text: His father-in-law, the girl’s father, persuaded him to stay, so he remained with him three days, eating, drinking, and lodging there.

familiar.text: And it came to pass on the fourth day, when they arose early in the morning, that he rose up to depart: and the damsel’s father said unto his son in law, Comfort thine heart with a morsel of bread, and afterward go your way.

modern.text: On the fourth day, they got up early in the morning and prepared to depart, but the girl’s father said to his son-in-law, “Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go.”

verses.restored: The two sat and ate and drank together. Father of young woman said to the man, Be willing, please, and lodge, and let your heart be good.

familiar.text: And they sat down, and did eat and drink both of them together: for the damsel’s father had said unto the man, Be content, I pray thee, and tarry all night, and let thine heart be merry.

modern.text: So they sat down and the two of them ate and drank together. Then the girl’s father said to the man, “Please agree to stay overnight and let your heart be merry.”

original.text: וַיֵּשְׁב֗וּ וַיֹּאכְל֧וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֛ם יַחְדָּ֖ו וַיִּשְׁתּ֑וּ וַיֹּ֜אמֶר אֲבִ֤י הַֽנַּעֲרָה֙ אֶל הָאִ֔ישׁ הֽוֹאֶל נָ֥א וְלִ֖ין וְיִטַ֥ב לִבֶּֽךָ

verses.restored: The man rose to go, but his father-in-law urged him, and he returned and lodged there.

familiar.text: And when the man rose up to depart, his father in law urged him: therefore he lodged there again.

modern.text: The man got up to depart, but his father-in-law persuaded him, so he stayed there that night.

original.text: וַיָּ֥קָם הָאִ֖ישׁ לָלֶ֑כֶת וַיִּפְצַר בּוֹ֙ חֹתְנ֔וֹ וַיָּ֖שָׁב וַיָּ֥לֶן שָֽׁם

verses.restored: He arose early in morning on fifth day to go. Father of young woman said, Strengthen your heart, please, and linger until day declines. The two of them ate.

familiar.text: And he arose early in the morning on the fifth day to depart: and the damsel’s father said, Comfort thine heart, I pray thee. And they tarried until afternoon, and they did eat both of them.

modern.text: On the fifth day, he got up early in the morning to depart, but the girl’s father said, “Please refresh your heart.” So they waited until late afternoon and the two of them ate.

original.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם בַּבֹּ֜קֶר בַּיּ֣וֹם הַחֲמִישִׁי֮ לָלֶכֶת֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲבִ֣י הַֽנַּעֲרָ֗ה סְעָד נָא֙ לְבָ֣בְךָ֔ וְהִֽתְמַהְמְה֖וּ עַד נְט֣וֹת הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּאכְל֖וּ שְׁנֵיהֶֽם

verses.restored: The man rose to go, he and his concubine and his servant. His father-in-law, father of young woman, said to him, Look, please, day has weakened toward evening. Lodge, please; look, day is encamping. Lodge here, and let your heart be good. Tomorrow arise early for your way, and go to your tent.

familiar.text: And when the man rose up to depart, he, and his concubine, and his servant, his father in law, the damsel’s father, said unto him, Behold, now the day draweth toward evening, I pray you tarry all night: behold, the day groweth to an end, lodge here, that thine heart may be merry; and to morrow get you early on your way, that thou mayest go home.

modern.text: When the man got up to depart with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the girl’s father, said to him, “Look, the day is drawing to a close. Please spend the night. See, the day is almost over. Spend the night here, that your heart may be merry. Then you can get up early tomorrow for your journey home.”

familiar.text: But the man would not tarry that night, but he rose up and departed, and came over against Jebus, which is Jerusalem; and there were with him two asses saddled, his concubine also was with him.

modern.text: But the man was unwilling to spend the night. He got up and departed, and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine.

modern.text: When they were near Jebus and the day was almost gone, the servant said to his master, “Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here.”

familiar.text: Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door, and spake to the master of the house, the old man, saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.

modern.text: While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly the wicked men of the city surrounded the house. Pounding on the door, they said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came to your house, so we can have relations with him!”

original.text: הֵמָּה֮ מֵיטִיבִ֣ים אֶת לִבָּם֒ וְהִנֵּה֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י הָעִ֜יר אַנְשֵׁ֣י בְנֵֽי בְלִיַּ֗עַל נָסַ֨בּוּ֙ אֶת הַבַּ֔יִת מִֽתְדַּפְּקִ֖ים עַל הַדָּ֑לֶת וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ אֶל הָ֠אִישׁ בַּ֣עַל הַבַּ֤יִת הַזָּקֵן֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הוֹצֵ֗א אֶת הָאִ֛ישׁ אֲשֶׁר בָּ֥א אֶל בֵּיתְךָ֖ וְנֵדָעֶֽנּוּ

verses.restored: The man, master of house, went out to them and said to them, No, my brothers, please do not act wickedly. After this man has come into my house, do not commit this outrage.

familiar.text: And the man, the master of the house, went out unto them, and said unto them, Nay, my brethren, nay, I pray you, do not so wickedly; seeing that this man is come into mine house, do not this folly.

modern.text: The owner of the house went out and said to them, “No, my brothers, do not do this wicked thing! After all, this man is a guest in my house. Do not commit this outrage.

original.text: וַיֵּצֵ֣א אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם הָאִישׁ֙ בַּ֣עַל הַבַּ֔יִת וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֔ם אַל אַחַ֖י אַל תָּרֵ֣עוּ נָ֑א אַ֠חֲרֵי אֲשֶׁר בָּ֞א הָאִ֤ישׁ הַזֶּה֙ אַל בֵּיתִ֔י אַֽל תַּעֲשׂ֖וּ אֶת הַנְּבָלָ֥ה הַזֹּֽאת

verses.restored: Look, my daughter, a virgin, and his concubine. Let me bring them out, please. Violate them and do to them what is good in your eyes; but against this man do not commit this outrageous thing.

familiar.text: Behold, here is my daughter a maiden, and his concubine; them I will bring out now, and humble ye them, and do with them what seemeth good unto you: but unto this man do not so vile a thing.

modern.text: Look, let me bring out my virgin daughter and the man’s concubine, and you can use them and do with them as you wish. But do not do such a vile thing to this man.”

original.text: הִנֵּה֩ בִתִּ֨י הַבְּתוּלָ֜ה וּפִֽילַגְשֵׁ֗הוּ אוֹצִֽיאָה נָּ֤א אוֹתָם֙ וְעַנּ֣וּ אוֹתָ֔ם וַעֲשׂ֣וּ לָהֶ֔ם הַטּ֖וֹב בְּעֵינֵיכֶ֑ם וְלָאִ֤ישׁ הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תַעֲשׂ֔וּ דְּבַ֖ר הַנְּבָלָ֥ה הַזֹּֽאת

verses.restored: The men were not willing to listen to him. The man seized his concubine and brought her out to them outside. They sexually knew her and abused her all night until morning, and they sent her away when dawn rose.

familiar.text: But the men would not hearken to him: so the man took his concubine, and brought her forth unto them; and they knew her, and abused her all the night until the morning: and when the day began to spring, they let her go.

modern.text: But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them, and they raped her and abused her throughout the night, and at dawn they let her go.

original.text: וְלֹֽא אָב֤וּ הָאֲנָשִׁים֙ לִשְׁמֹ֣עַֽ ל֔וֹ וַיַּחֲזֵ֤ק הָאִישׁ֙ בְּפִ֣ילַגְשׁ֔וֹ וַיֹּצֵ֥א אֲלֵיהֶ֖ם הַח֑וּץ וַיֵּדְע֣וּ א֠וֹתָהּ וַיִּֽתְעַלְּלוּ בָ֤הּ כָּל הַלַּ֨יְלָה֙ עַד הַבֹּ֔קֶר וַֽיְשַׁלְּח֖וּהָ בעלות הַשָּֽׁחַר

verses.restored: The woman came toward turning of morning and fell at entrance of house of the man where her lord was, until light.

familiar.text: Then came the woman in the dawning of the day, and fell down at the door of the man’s house where her lord was, till it was light.

modern.text: Early that morning, the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light.

original.text: וַתָּבֹ֥א הָאִשָּׁ֖ה לִפְנ֣וֹת הַבֹּ֑קֶר וַתִּפֹּ֞ל פֶּ֧תַח בֵּית הָאִ֛ישׁ אֲשֶׁר אֲדוֹנֶ֥יהָ שָּׁ֖ם עַד הָאֽוֹר

verses.restored: Her lord arose in morning, opened doors of house, and went out to go on his way. Look, the woman, his concubine, was fallen at entrance of house, and her hands were upon threshold.

familiar.text: And her lord rose up in the morning, and opened the doors of the house, and went out to go his way: and, behold, the woman his concubine was fallen down at the door of the house, and her hands were upon the threshold.

modern.text: In the morning, when her master got up and opened the doors of the house to go out on his journey, there was his concubine, collapsed in the doorway of the house, with her hands on the threshold.

original.text: וַיָּ֨קָם אֲדֹנֶ֜יהָ בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּפְתַּח֙ דַּלְת֣וֹת הַבַּ֔יִת וַיֵּצֵ֖א לָלֶ֣כֶת לְדַרְכּ֑וֹ וְהִנֵּ֧ה הָאִשָּׁ֣ה פִֽילַגְשׁ֗וֹ נֹפֶ֨לֶת֙ פֶּ֣תַח הַבַּ֔יִת וְיָדֶ֖יהָ עַל הַסַּֽף

verses.restored: He said to her, Arise, and let us go. There was no answer. He took her upon donkey, and the man arose and went to his place.

familiar.text: And he said unto her, Up, and let us be going. But none answered. Then the man took her up upon an ass, and the man rose up, and gat him unto his place.

modern.text: “Get up,” he told her. “Let us go.” But there was no response. So the man put her on his donkey and set out for home.

original.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר אֵלֶ֛יהָ ק֥וּמִי וְנֵלֵ֖כָה וְאֵ֣ין עֹנֶ֑ה וַיִּקָּחֶ֨הָ֙ עַֽל הַחֲמ֔וֹר וַיָּ֣קָם הָאִ֔ישׁ וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ לִמְקֹמֽוֹ

verses.restored: He came to his house, took the knife, seized body of his concubine, and cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces. He sent her throughout all territory of Israel.

familiar.text: And when he was come into his house, he took a knife, and laid hold on his concubine, and divided her, together with her bones, into twelve pieces, and sent her into all the coasts of Israel.

modern.text: When he reached his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout the territory of Israel.

original.text: וַיָּבֹ֣א אֶל בֵּית֗וֹ וַיִּקַּ֤ח אֶת הַֽמַּאֲכֶ֨לֶת֙ וַיַּחֲזֵ֣ק בְּפִֽילַגְשׁ֔וֹ וַֽיְנַתְּחֶ֨הָ֙ לַעֲצָמֶ֔יהָ לִשְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר נְתָחִ֑ים וַֽיְשַׁלְּחֶ֔הָ בְּכֹ֖ל גְּב֥וּל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

verses.restored: Everyone who saw said, Such a thing has not happened and has not been seen from day children of Israel came up from land of Egypt to this day. Set your heart upon it; take counsel and speak.

familiar.text: And it was so, that all that saw it said, There was no such deed done nor seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt unto this day: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds.

modern.text: And everyone who saw it said, “Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!”

original.text: וְהָיָ֣ה כָל הָרֹאֶ֗ה וְאָמַר֙ לֹֽא נִהְיְתָ֤ה וְלֹֽא נִרְאֲתָה֙ כָּזֹ֔את לְמִיּ֞וֹם עֲל֤וֹת בְּנֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם עַ֖ד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה שִֽׂימוּ לָכֶ֥ם עָלֶ֖יהָ עֻ֥צוּ וְדַבֵּֽרוּ

translation_notes: The woman is never named. 'Concubine' translates pilegesh, a recognized but structurally subordinate partner status. That status never reduces her humanity, consent, bodily autonomy, or right to safety.

Verse 2 has a major witness difference. Masoretic Hebrew uses zanah, often read as sexual unfaithfulness, while Greek witnesses describe anger or estrangement. Neither reading causes, excuses, or morally prepares the violence later committed against her.

The Levite goes 'to speak to her heart,' language of persuasion or reconciliation, but the narrative never records her speech or explicit consent to return. Her father's hospitality cannot substitute for her decision.

The Levite refuses a Jebusite city because its residents are not Israelites and chooses Gibeah. The resulting atrocity deliberately destroys any claim that in-group identity guarantees moral safety or that foreigners are inherently more dangerous.
Gibeah's failure begins before the assault: travelers sit in the square without welcome. Hospitality is not merely private courtesy here; social abandonment leaves vulnerable people exposed.

The mob demands sexual domination of the male guest. The host condemns this while offering his daughter and the concubine instead. Protecting one person by surrendering women to rape is itself monstrous, not hospitality or lesser harm.

Verse 24 preserves the host's words, 'do what is good in your eyes,' echoing the book's moral refrain in a scene where patriarchal judgment treats women's bodies as negotiable. The text reports this collapse; it does not endorse it.
Verse 25 states that the Levite seizes and puts his concubine outside. She is not a voluntary substitute and cannot be blamed for violence inflicted by the mob, host, Levite, city, or social order.
The verbs describe repeated sexual assault and abuse through the night. Translation should be direct enough to resist euphemism but must not sensationalize or turn her trauma into spectacle.

Her hands on the threshold preserve a final bodily image of seeking shelter from the house that failed her. Whether she died before or after the Levite's later action has been debated, but the received narrative gives no answering voice.

The command 'Arise, and let us go' displays profound callousness toward a catastrophically injured or dead woman. It must not be used to portray trauma survivors as unresponsive, disobedient, or spiritually deficient.

The Levite dismembers and distributes her body without recorded consent, transforming her again into an instrument for male political mobilization. National outrage does not restore her name, voice, or bodily integrity.

The summons frames the event as unprecedented outrage, yet the following chapters redirect grief into war and further violence against women. Moral shock without survivor-centered justice can become another engine of domination.
safety_note: Maximum anti-sexual-violence and anti-trauma safeguards: Do not blame the unnamed woman, eroticize the assault, excuse the host or Levite, or call her surrender a sacrifice. Her relationship status, possible estrangement, travel, sexuality, silence, injury, and death never authorize abuse. Do not preach that hospitality requires surrendering women, that male rape is uniquely shameful, or that collective revenge repairs sexual violence. Center her stolen safety, voice, body, and dignity, and refuse every use of this chapter against women, queer people, migrants, sex workers, trauma survivors, or any targeted group.
